title: Integration discovery - Lucid Systems
summary: Initial integration discovery for Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private. Focus on SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy pattern, rate limiting, and observability hooks. Customer is evaluating deployment options for a customer-facing semantic search + chat product; primary concerns are latency, token cost, and VPC networking. Agreed next steps: send SDK code samples, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter guide, security whitepaper, and schedule a 1-hour POC scoping with infra team next week.
topics: Rate limits, quotas and burst behaviour
Observability hooks, tracing, and cost telemetry
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-07 16:00 UTC | Duration ~45m | Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (CTO, Lucid), Ben Rhodes (Lead ML Eng, Lucid), Sara Lim (Infra Arch, Lucid)

00:00 Alyssa: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
00:05 Maya: yep, loud and clear, thanks Alyssa.
00:10 Alyssa: cool, quick agenda — we want to understand your integration surface, SDKs, any LangChain/LlamaIndex usage, how you plan proxy/gateway and rate limits, and what observability you need. Ravi will jump into a couple of technical slides and we've got time for Qs then next steps.
00:30 Ben: sounds good. to set context we are building semantic search + a chat widget for customers — mostly multi-tenant. currently prototype uses OpenAI endpoint via our API gateway, but cost and latency are creeping up as we scale. looking at Redwood for better economics and more deployment options.
00:50 Ravi: great, thanks. can you tell us about your stack — where models are called from, any SDKs you already use, and if you're using LangChain or LlamaIndex wrappers?
01:05 Ben: primarily Node backend microservices on AWS, we have a serverless edge for the widget calls (lambda@edge) and a mid-tier in ECS; data pipeline's in k8s. Not using LangChain in prod right now, but we prototyped with LlamaIndex locally. Our devs like the chaining primitives.
01:30 Sara: infra wise we have a VPC per environment, strict egress rules, and we need to pass traffic through our corporate gateway for logging. we also have compliance reqs — SOC2 in progress, and PII retention rules.
01:50 Alyssa: got it — so three threads: SDK ergonomics (we have JS/TS and Python SDKs), LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, and network/proxy patterns. quick Q: is low single-digit 100s of ms latency a hard SLO?
02:10 Maya: for the chat UX we want sub-500ms on short responses; search can tolerate 500-800ms. bursty traffic is a concern though — Black Friday-style spikes could be 5-10x.
02:30 Ravi: thanks. on SDKs: Redwood has official JS/TS and Python SDKs with streaming support and built-in retry/backoff. we also have example adapters for LangChain and LlamaIndex — the adapters keep tokenization and prompt templates consistent and support callback hooks for tracing. here's a link to the adapter repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/langchain-adapters (note: example link)
02:55 Ben: nice, does the adapter maintain KV cache compatibility if we switch model variants? in our proto we cache embeddings and reuse KV for chat context.
03:12 Ravi: good point — we expose a per-request metadata header that maps to Redwood's cache keys; the runtime will do prefix/KV cache when supported. switching model variants keeps the cache key mapping if you set the model alias — we can share a doc.
03:30 Sara: networking — we don't want to allow outbound calls from our VPC directly to hosted endpoints, so we'd prefer a gateway/proxy pattern. do you have recommended proxy patterns or a sidecar?
03:45 Alyssa: common pattern: customer runs a lightweight gateway/proxy in their VPC that authenticates to Redwood with a short-lived mTLS or token, and it forwards requests. For Dedicated and Private deployments you can run the inference endpoint inside the VPC to avoid egress. we have a sample k8s helm chart and a proxy example that integrates with Kong/Envoy. we'll share the snippet.
04:10 Ben: for the hosted API path, can we route through our gateway and have rate limiting enforced by Redwood as well? we want per-tenant quotas and global quotas.
04:25 Ravi: yes — Redwood supports per-api-key and per-route quotas. you can set quotas tied to your tenant id via metadata headers or use multiple API keys per tenant. burst window and smoothing policies are configurable (e.g., token-per-minute + burst credits). we also support a gateway mode where your proxy authenticates and acts as the single key but passes tenant id in headers; Redwood will meter and invoice by tenant if configured.
04:55 Sara: what about observability — we need request-level traces, token cost, latency, and partial streaming traces for debugging.
05:10 Ravi: Redwood Console exposes per-route token counts, latency percentiles, and trace ids that you can forward into your tracing backend (Datadog/Jaeger). SDKs have callback hooks for start/end/stream-chunk and we emit a trace-id header (x-rw-trace-id) so you can correlate logs. there is also a webhooks API for post-call events with cost and usage.
05:40 Maya: are those hooks safe for PII? we can't include full prompt text in webhook if it's customer PII.
05:50 Alyssa: good catch — webhooks can omit prompt bodies and only include hashes and token counts; we also have redact rules and a retention/ttl policy. For Private deployments, you can disable telemetry or host the control plane with customer-managed storage.
06:10 Ben: about LangChain — do you support streaming callbacks into LangChain Agents and the run managers? we liked the run-level metadata in LC for evals.
06:25 Ravi: yes — our LangChain integrations implement the callback manager interfaces, so runs show up and streaming chunks are forwarded. LlamaIndex connector is also available; it preserves the document ids and embedding metadata so your vector DB integrations remain consistent. example: https://redwood.example.com/docs/langchain-integration
06:45 Ben: cool. how invasive is integration — we want minimal refactor. ideally swap out the transport layer.
06:55 Ravi: in most cases it's a small transport shim. for Node the SDK replaces the fetch call, and adapters wrap the higher-level classes. we can share a migration recipe (3-4 files).
07:10 Sara: security/compliance — what's the SOC2 story and key management options? we need customer-managed KMS for Private, and audit logs for Dedicated.
07:25 Alyssa: Redwood has SOC2 Type II in place (link to attestation), Dedicated gets audit logging and optional customer-managed KMS via AWS KMS or GCP KMS; Private gives full control. we'll send the security whitepaper and SOC2 report under NDA.
07:40 Maya: pricing — are there hidden costs for streaming or connection counts?
07:48 Alyssa: streaming is billed per token plus a small per-connection minute charge for long-lived streams; Dedicated has predictable throughput pricing (reserved GPU hours) so unit token cost is lower at scale. Optimize tooling suggests batching/quantization to reduce cost. We'll include an example cost model for your expected qps.
08:10 Ben: curious about fallbacks — if our primary model variant is busy, can you auto-fallback to a cheaper variant with same API?
08:20 Ravi: yes — routing policies support fallbacks by model alias and cost tier. you can set latency or cost thresholds and Redwood will route to a compatible model. it's plumbed through the SDK so your code doesn't change.
08:35 Maya: what about rate-limiting behavior — do you drop requests or queue them? we need predictable client behavior.
08:45 Ravi: we offer both: hard quotas return 429 immediately. soft quotas can queue for a configurable time window (e.g., 3s) and accept with a 206 style partial or delayed response. for chat low-latency paths we recommend soft smoothing plus circuit-breaker at proxy level.
09:05 Ben: are there any gotchas with lambda@edge or serverless frontends?
09:12 Ravi: yes — long-lived connections and streaming can be tricky with Lambda@Edge. strategy: keep the widget connection to your edge and fan-out to Redwood from a mid-tier that supports streaming (ECS/Fargate). we can share an example architecture diagram.
09:30 Sara: on quotas, can we set per-tenant monthly caps and webhook when nearing cap?
09:38 Alyssa: yes — billing hooks and webhooks can notify you at thresholds. you can also set hard cutoffs per tenant.
09:45 Ben: ok, deployment options — for Dedicated we get reserved GPU capacity, right? how long to provision?
09:53 Alyssa: typically 2-3 weeks for initial capacity provisioning once the contract and region are finalized; Private on-prem will vary (4-8 weeks) depending on rack/hardware. Dedicated also supports autoscale and burst policies into hosted pool.
10:12 Maya: we'd like to do a POC that includes an A/B with current OpenAI path for latency and cost. can Redwood run a benchmark harness?
10:22 Ravi: absolutely — we have a lightweight benchmark harness and a perf spreadsheet. we can run per-token latency and cost breakdowns against your prompts and seq lengths. we'll need sample prompts and a small dataset (anonymized).
10:40 Maya: we'll prepare 200 representative prompts and a synthetic traffic pattern. timeline: we'd like POC next week if possible.
10:50 Alyssa: great — proposed next steps: 1) send SDK + LangChain/LlamaIndex code samples, 2) security whitepaper and SOC2, 3) sample proxy helm chart, 4) benchmark harness and perf spreadsheet, 5) schedule POC scoping call with your infra on Tue 2026-05-12.
11:10 Ben: sounds good. one more quick question — can we get per-request cost metadata in the response so we can attribute spending to tenant and feature?
11:20 Ravi: yes, we have response headers that include token counts and estimated cost; you can also pull per-call line items from the usage API.
11:30 Sara: ok thanks everyone.
11:35 Alyssa: thanks all we'll follow up with the materials and invite.
11:40 Maya: thanks, bye.

Notes: transcript includes occasional minor mis-hearings and shorthand; speaker labels are mostly accurate. references to URLs are placeholders and will be replaced with final links in follow-up.
